summary: For ages 7–9, teach predator hunting and prey defence as a matched two-sided contest rather than a one-way menace: anchor at least three hunting strategies (ambush/lie-in-wait, pursuit/speed, pack/cooperative hunting, trap-building like a spider web, stealth/camouflage, tool/tongue or venom) each paired with the prey defence that counters it (camouflage, speed/agility, armour/spines, warning colours, group living, playing dead, mimicry, confusing patterns). Build toward the 'arms race' idea — a better hunting trick pressures prey to defend better, which pressures hunters again — kept concrete and non-technical. Crucially, frame improvement as happening across many generations (faster survivors have more young), not within one animal's lifetime, and frame predators as survivors solving a problem, not villains.
misconceptions: 'Predators always win / are cruel villains' — hunting is a survival need and most hunts fail.
'All predators just chase and bite' — many ambush, trap, cooperate, or use venom instead of speed.
'Prey are helpless' — prey have powerful defences (camouflage, speed, armour, warning colours, numbers).
'Warning colours help prey hide' — bright warning colours ADVERTISE danger (toxicity), the opposite of camouflage.
'One animal evolves to win permanently' — improvements on one side pressure the other, so neither side stays ahead (arms race).

activities.title: Hunt-or-hide matchup: pair each strategy with its counter
steps: Lay out cards or a board with predator strategies on one side (ambush, pursuit, pack-hunt, trap/web, tongue/venom) and prey defences on the other (camouflage, speed/agility, armour/spines, warning colours, herd/group living, confusing patterns).

For each pairing, say out loud who you think usually prevails and why, then check: ambush often succeeds against a dozing, inattentive grazer; staying alert and vigilant makes an ambush less likely to succeed; armour or spines can put off a single biter; a cooperating pack can overwhelm a lone defender, while bunching together in a group helps prey resist a pack; speed is often answered by agility and sharp turns.

Match at least three hunting strategies to the prey defence that works against each one, and name a real animal example for both sides (e.g. crocodile ambush at the water's edge vs an alert, watchful herd; cheetah pursuit vs a gazelle's speed and swerves; wolf pack vs musk oxen that bunch together in a defensive group; spider web trap vs an insect that detects and avoids the strands; a chameleon's long sticky tongue vs insects that are camouflaged or stay hidden; a lone biter vs a porcupine's spines or a skunk's spray; a chasing predator vs zebra stripes, which some scientists think may make a running herd harder to pick out, though this is still debated).
activities.insight: Hunting and defence often come in matched pairs — many attacking tricks are met by defences that work against them — so 'predator' is not just 'fast and toothy' and prey are far from helpless.

activities.title: Camouflage grab game: why hidden prey survive
steps: Spread coloured paper dots (or sweets) over a patterned cloth — some dots matching the pattern, some standing out clearly.
Before playing, predict out loud which colours will survive and which will be grabbed.
Acting as the 'predator', take 10 seconds to grab as many dots as you can, then count which colours were left behind.

Discuss: compare your result with your prediction. If the well-camouflaged dots mostly survived, then, if these were real prey, the hidden ones would be more likely to live and have young that inherit their colouring. If they did not, talk about why (for example, the time limit, or how the dots were spread out).
activities.insight: Camouflage gives a real survival advantage, and because the better-hidden individuals survive to reproduce, their colouring becomes more common over generations — the raw material of the arms race.

activities.title: Spot the hidden hunter (and hidden prey)
steps: Look at a scene (a drawn or photographed picture) where an ambush predator OR camouflaged prey is hidden against a matching background.
Point to where you think the hidden animal is, and say which clues gave it away.

Say whether this is a hunting advantage (the predator stays unseen until it strikes) or a defence advantage (the prey stays unseen so it is not found), and explain which side camouflage is helping in this picture.
activities.insight: The same trick — blending into the background — can serve either the hunter (ambush) or the hunted (hiding), showing camouflage as a tool both sides can use.

activities.title: Run the escalation: the arms-race ladder
steps: Start with a before-and-after story: a group of gazelles includes a few that happen to be a little faster. When cheetahs hunt, the slower gazelles are caught more often and the faster ones escape and survive to have young.
Say what the gazelle group looks like after many generations (faster on average), then ask which cheetahs now catch enough food (the faster ones), and what their offspring are like.

Step this up a ladder: faster prey over generations → the faster hunters are the ones that survive → prey that are faster still survive best → and so on, each rung a new generation, not a new trick learned in one lifetime.
State in your own words why there is no permanent winner: whenever one side improves, the survivors on the other side are the ones who can still cope, so both keep being pushed to improve.

Optional: if an interactive simulation or matchup is available, run repeated encounters and watch the losing side 'upgrade' a trait so the outcome flips — but describe each upgrade as the faster/better-defended individuals surviving and having young over many generations, not one animal changing its own body.
activities.insight: A predator-prey 'arms race' is a reciprocal, many-generations process: improvements on one side pressure the other, so neither gains a permanent advantage, and the build-up of speed or defence happens across generations, never within a single animal's lifetime.

activities.title: Sort and explain: checking the pairings and the 'no villain' idea
steps: Sort a set of animals by how the predators hunt (ambush / pursuit / pack / trap / tongue or venom) and by how the prey defend (camouflage / speed / armour or spines / warning colours / group living).
For each predator, say why it hunts — to eat and survive — and judge the claim 'the predator is a bad animal for hunting' (it is not; hunting is how it feeds).
Answer and justify: why does no side win permanently? (Because every improvement on one side pressures the other to improve across generations.)
activities.insight: Predation is feeding and survival, not malice, and the two-sided pressure means neither side holds a lasting advantage.

checkQuestion: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals, and the gazelles they hunt are also very fast — almost as fast as the cheetah. Why would the prey be nearly as fast as the predator chasing it? Where did all that speed come from?
checkAnswer: Over very many generations, the gazelles that happened to be a bit faster were the ones that escaped and survived to have young, so gazelles as a group became faster and faster. That made them harder to catch, so the faster cheetahs were the ones that caught enough food and survived — and cheetahs got faster too. Each side keeps pushing the other to improve. That back-and-forth over generations is the 'arms race' between predator and prey; the speed built up across many generations, not in one animal's lifetime.
